c.tagline: Guadeloupe's breezy resort town of Creole beaches and its offshore islet.

taxi.fareNote: Taxis are metered but expensive, with surcharges at night, on Sundays, and on holidays. There is no Uber; the Heetch app has some coverage, but renting a car is by far the most practical way to explore the island.

emergency.note: 112 reaches all emergency services across this French overseas department; or dial 17 for police, 15 for ambulance (SAMU), and 18 for fire.

hood_landmark.Pointe de la Verdure: Pointe de la Verdure Le Gosier beach

avoid.reason: Le Gosier itself has no no-go areas, but avoid downtown Pointe-à-Pitre and its Lauricisque district nearby after dark.
Car break-ins at beach parking lots such as Plage de la Datcha — leave nothing visible in vehicles.

hood_desc: The lively heart of Le Gosier, with a small waterfront, a market, restaurants, and a jetty where boats shuttle across to the Îlet du Gosier and its little lighthouse; the most convenient base for staying without a car.

A marina district on the edge of Pointe-à-Pitre, packed with waterfront restaurants and bars, the Aquarium of Guadeloupe, and the historic Fort Fleur d'Épée on the hill above; best for dining and going out.
Le Gosier's main hotel strip, a leafy peninsula of resort hotels, a casino, and calm swimming beaches; suits travellers who want to walk straight to the sand and dine at the resorts.
A quieter residential neighbourhood set back on the hillside with views over the bay, home to the landmark Auberge de la Vieille Tour in a converted 18th-century windmill; calm and scenic.
A relaxed area east of the town known for the sheltered cove beaches of Petit-Havre and nearby Anse Tabarin; quiet, local, and family-friendly, but a car makes it far easier.

water.note: Tap water is treated and generally safe, though outages and post-storm advisories make many keep bottled on hand.

transit.hours: Buses generally run from around 5:30 AM to 8:00 PM Monday to Friday, with reduced service on Saturday mornings and little to nothing on Sundays.
transit.note: Public transport is the Karu'lis network, serving Cap Excellence (Les Abymes, Baie-Mahault, Pointe-à-Pitre) and the Riviera du Levant (Le Gosier, Sainte-Anne, Saint-François); independent carriers cover other routes on looser schedules. There is no rail. Because buses stop early and don't run Sundays, most visitors rent a car.
transit.pay: Buy a ticket from the driver in cash; fares start around €1.20 depending on the zone.

bus: Independent carriers to other Grande-Terre and Basse-Terre towns
ferry: Boat shuttle from Le Gosier bourg to the Îlet du Gosier
Inter-island ferries from Pointe-à-Pitre to Marie-Galante, Les Saintes and La Désirade

transit.m: Karu'lis bus toward Le Gosier (hourly, roughly 5:40 AM - 6:50 PM)
Taxi to Le Gosier (15-20 min; surcharges at night and Sundays)

tip.r: Service is included by law (service compris); rounding up or leaving a euro or two for good service is a kind gesture but not expected.

food.name: Accras de morue
food.desc: Salt cod fritters seasoned with chive, chilli and garlic, deep fried to order and eaten hot with a squeeze of lime and chien sauce.

places.name: Chez Meme
places.note: Family Creole kitchen whose cod accras get named alongside its colombo.

places.name: Snack Delices
places.note: Traditional snack address for accras, bokits and colombo at local prices.

places.name: Lolos on Plage de la Datcha
places.note: Beach shacks fry accras through the afternoon; cheapest and freshest way to try them.

food.name: Colombo de poulet or cabri
food.desc: Chicken or goat stewed in Guadeloupe's own curry blend with potato, aubergine and mango, served with rice and red beans.

places.name: Chez Meme

places.name: Snack Delices

places.name: Restaurant-Bar La Verdure

food.name: Boudin creole
food.desc: Spiced blood sausage bound with bread, onion and hot pepper, poached and eaten in short lengths as an aperitif with accras and a ti-punch.

places.note: Market vendors sell boudin by the metre in the morning; ask for it warm.

places.name: Lolos on Plage de la Datcha
places.note: Beach shacks pair boudin with a cold Lorraine beer at sundown.

food.name: Bokit
food.desc: Guadeloupe's street sandwich: dough fried until puffed and golden, split and stuffed with salt cod, chicken, cheese or conch and plenty of sauce chien.

places.name: Bokit Center
places.note: Dedicated bokit shop using a lighter dough and fresh seasonal fillings.

places.name: Snack Delices
places.note: Reliable bokits alongside the rest of the Creole snack menu.

places.name: Roadside vans along the Gosier seafront
places.note: Evening bokit vans are a Guadeloupean ritual; expect a queue and a wait.

food.name: Poulet boucane
food.desc: Chicken marinated in Creole spices and smoked slowly over sugarcane leaves, chopped and served with sauce chien, rice and fried plantain.

places.name: Restaurant-Bar La Verdure
places.note: Sit-down version with the smoked chicken served as a full plate.

food.name: Court-bouillon and blaff de poisson
food.desc: Local reef fish either simmered in a tomato, lime and chilli court-bouillon or poached blaff-style in a sharp garlicky broth with wild thyme.

places.name: Casa Datcha
places.note: Beachfront tables looking across to Ilet du Gosier; fish of the day is the order.

places.name: Coconut Coast
places.note: Creole seafood cooking including langouste and fresh catch, lunch and dinner.

places.name: Marche du Gosier
places.note: Buy the fish yourself in the morning and see what the day's catch actually is.

food.name: Ti-punch
food.desc: The island aperitif: white rhum agricole, a spoon of cane syrup and a twist of lime peel, stirred and served without ice, chacun prepare la sienne.

places.name: Casa Datcha
places.note: Sunset ti-punch and cocktails with the islet in view; the classic Gosier moment.

places.name: Restaurant-Bar La Verdure
places.note: Bar side pours ti-punch and rum arranges made in-house.

places.name: Lolos on Plage de la Datcha

food.name: Jus locaux
food.desc: Fresh cane juice, plus maracudja, corossol and goyave juices pressed from island fruit; the non-alcoholic staple of every Creole meal.

landmarks: Îlet du Gosier
A postcard islet just offshore crowned by a red-topped 19th-century lighthouse, reached by kayak or shuttle boat for swimming beneath coconut palms.
Fort Fleur d'Épée
An 18th-century hilltop fortress fought over by French and British forces, its ramparts, tunnels and gardens now overlook the entire bay.
Plage de la Datcha
Le Gosier's lively town beach facing the islet, where families picnic under sea-grape trees and food trucks serve bokits at sunset.
Aquarium de la Guadeloupe
The Caribbean's noted aquarium at Bas du Fort, showcasing sharks, sea turtles and mangrove ecosystems with a strong marine-conservation mission.
Marina Bas du Fort
One of the Caribbean's largest marinas, a bustling harbor village of a thousand yachts, waterside restaurants and boutiques between Gosier and Pointe-à-Pitre.
Pointe de la Verdure
Le Gosier's resort headland of hotel beaches, casino and spa, where calm lagoon waters and palm groves define Guadeloupe's riviera.
Plage de Saint-Félix
A quieter golden cove east of town, favored by locals for weekend swims and shaded by almond trees away from the resort bustle.
Église Saint-Louis du Gosier
The commune's landmark parish church, whose bell tower presides over the market square and generations of Gosier's town life.
Friday Night Market of Gosier
A weekly evening street fair by the waterfront where Creole musicians, rum stalls and grilled-lobster vendors turn the town center festive.
Étang du Mitan
A mangrove-fringed pond behind the coast where kayakers and paddleboarders glide past wetland birds and hidden coves close to Le Gosier's beaches.

train.note: There is no railway anywhere in Guadeloupe - the last of the sugar-estate lines closed decades ago - so no trains serve Le Gosier or any other commune, and there is nothing to connect to internationally. Travel around the island is entirely by road, and between islands by ferry or air from Pointe-à-Pitre's Guadeloupe Pôle Caraïbes airport.

bus.note: Le Gosier is about 6 km east of Pointe-à-Pitre and is served by the island's public bus network, branded Karu'lis in the Pointe-à-Pitre conurbation, with frequent runs along the coast road into the Bergevin and Darboussier stops in town; most Guadeloupe routes radiate from Pointe-à-Pitre. Fares are paid to the driver in cash and services thin out sharply in the evenings and at weekends, especially on Sundays. Being an island, Guadeloupe has no international buses and no long-distance coach network, so hire cars, taxis and the ferries fill the gaps.

intl.to: Roseau (Dominica), Fort-de-France & Le Marin (Martinique), Castries (Saint Lucia) - sails from the Gare Maritime de Bergevin in Pointe-à-Pitre, about 15 minutes from Le Gosier
Grand-Bourg, Marie-Galante & Terre-de-Haut and Terre-de-Bas, Les Saintes (Guadeloupe) - from the Pointe-à-Pitre ferry terminal
Îlet du Gosier (Guadeloupe) - shuttle boats from the beach jetty at Le Gosier, about 5 minutes
intl.op: local navette operators — tickets bought at the jetty

ferry.note: Almost everything leaves from the Gare Maritime de Bergevin in Pointe-à-Pitre, a short drive or bus ride from Le Gosier, with Val'Ferry and Jeans for Freedom competing on the Marie-Galante and Les Saintes runs and CTM Deher sailing to Les Saintes from Trois-Rivières on Basse-Terre, which is the shortest crossing. Reckon on about 45-60 minutes to Marie-Galante, roughly an hour to Les Saintes, around 2 hours to Dominica and 3.5-4 hours to Martinique. The international sailings need a passport or EU identity card and check-in an hour before departure. Crossings can be rough or cancelled in heavy swell and during the June-November hurricane season, so book online ahead in high season and around Carnival.

half.name: Mémorial ACTe
half.blurb: The monumental silver-latticed museum of slavery and Caribbean memory on Pointe-à-Pitre's waterfront, minutes away and among the region's essential cultural sites.
